utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the witness now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, I think we are on cross-examination, or are we still leading?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We are still on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Guiding. Sir, yesterday in your testimony you referred to Mr Landzo, called Zenga. Did you know Mr Landzo before you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (in interpretation): No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure we have reminded him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I will continue to speak the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How did you know -- how did you learn who Mr Landzo was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found that out from the others who were in Number 6, and the nickname "Zenga" I found out very quickly, and later I found his name and last name.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How often would you see Zenga at the camp approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was his function at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had the role of a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe what he looked like in 1992, while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was shortish. He often had his head shaved, and then he also shaved the sides above the ears and was leaving the top, and then later he shaved his whole head. He was bald.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you recollect: was he there your entire time that you were in Celebici, or was there a time when you no longer saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a time, and I can't recall the month now, he went somewhere, and then later he reappeared with a white belt. He came on two or three occasions, and was taking out Dusko Bendjo. I don't know what they were talking about, but after that I heard that he was calling him for some German Marks, but he was not appearing at the camp, only at the gate, and then he would leave. I think that was in late August, early September.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, you also mentioned Hazim Delic. Did you know Mr Delic before you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How did he learn who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second day after I was put in Number 6, when we went out, he was sitting to the right, that is the left-hand side, and you could recognise him really well because of the crutches he had on, and I asked Radoslav Vujcic who it was, and he told me it was him. Later I could recognise him because of the crutches. His name -- that is the second -- since the second day I knew his name.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately how long did Mr Delic have crutches, if you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember how long. He had it on for a while, and he sat in Number 6 on a crate down on the right-hand side somewhere to the right, against the tin wall, but I don't know how long it was, because a lot of time has passed since all this occurred, but it was a short period of time. I don't know how long.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe him besides the fact in the beginning he had crutches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was well-built, tall. He also had his hair cut short. At first he had one pistol and one automatic rifle, which was fairly short. It was like a machine gun or something. Then he had an automatic rifle. Then he had another pistol, a bit longer one, on the other side. When we walked, he walked swaggering with his arms apart.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How often would you see Mr Delic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every day. He would come every morning to the camp, not the same time every morning, but every morning just about he would come.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know what his function was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the guards had -- the guard --

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Can we stop for one minute. I believe we missed some of that last translation. I don't know if the translator can repeat it. I need to have the witness start from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Me too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You want to start where it was ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, sir. Because of a problem with the equipment, those of us who do not understand your language did not hear your response. Can you once again start from the beginning and answer, if you know, what Mr Delic's function in the camp was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role of Mr Delic, of Delic, I don't know what it was, but I know that when he would appear, we had to get up, and the guards told us when he would appear. They said: "Here comes the boss", and he would come every morning, and based on that I think that most probably he was the Deputy Commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see his relationship with the other guards? Were the other guards ever giving him instructions, or vice versa; he was giving the guards instructions, the other guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was issuing orders to other guards. I can give you an example that I remember very bell: it relates to what I was talking about yesterday. When the policemen were killed near Repovci and later on it was found out it was the Muslims who killed them, he ordered Landzo that this would be breakfast, lunch and dinner for the people of Bradina, and Landzo carried out his orders after that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In addition to what you observed about Mr Delic while you were at the camp, did you learn anything else about who had any responsibility or position in Celebici? For instance, did you ever learn who was in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found out that the head of the camp was Pavo Mucic and that Delic was his deputy. I heard that from people who knew them very well and from our people who were on the outside, and who were delivering us food. For instance, Nenad Kujundic and then Davor Bendjo and others, because when the camp Commander would come, and I only saw him three times, first Hazim Delic would come and would tell us to get up, because the Commander was coming, so we had to get up, and he would go from one person to the next, and I saw him on three occasions in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when it was that you saw Mr Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately some time in late June or early July. I wouldn't know exactly. It was after a group was released, and he came then. We got up, and he separated out the sick ones and the elderly and took them somewhere, and later we heard from Nenad and from Bendjo that the guards told them that they would be transferred to Musala. The second time there was a second group that also left. He also came. We got up. He read the names out, and he took them away. The third group, that was the group where I was in, that was mid-October, that was on 8th October, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Even if you did not see him personally, did you ever hear, while you were at the camp, that Mucic was present in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard, while I was in the camp, that on one occasion even those who knew him a bit better, when we were beaten, they thought about asking Pavo Mucic whether he knew about these murders and these beatings that were taking place, and to complain to him, but nobody dared ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from the guards or from noises outside any indication that Mr Mucic was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know how Mr Mucic would arrive at the camp, what transportation he would use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. To Number 6 he would mostly come on a motorcycle, and I could learn that from the guards. When you heard the sound of the motorcycle, they would say: "Here comes the Commander." They would say: "Just put your hands on your knees." But he would not come in, but from those who were outside, we heard that he did come.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, without giving the names of any of the prisoners involved, can you tell the court whether or not you ever observed any sexual mistreatment while you were at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Two brothers were brought in later --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. The question was whether he ever received any sexual treatment at Celebici. He is not answering her question. Non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If counsel will check her transcript, my question was whether or not he observed any sexual mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I apologise. Ms McHenry is correct. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, again, please without giving the names of anyone involved, please tell us what you observed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw two brothers, to whom the guard ordered to put their sexual organs into each other's mouths.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where did this occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Hangar Number 6 in front of all of us. I think there were over 200 of us there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember who the guard involved was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was the guard involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Landzo, Esad Landzo, called Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever see any prisoners mistreated by use of a detonation cord?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can he give us an approximate date when this thing happened, May, June, July; when?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going back to the incident where the persons were made to put their sexual organs into each other's mouths, if you know, approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I know that it was day-time, but I don't know the time.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what month it was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall. They were brought in after us. That could be late June or early July. I cannot tell you exactly, but I remember it as if I were seeing it now.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Just to clarify, were they brought in in late June or early July, as best you can remember, or is late June or early July when the incident happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were brought in after us, maybe fifteen, twenty days after us, and they were first beaten and then that was -- I don't know exactly. I think it was early July, maybe late June. I couldn't answer precisely to that question, because a lot of time has passed and I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Sir, did you ever observe any mistreatment with use of a detonation cord?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why are you suggesting the nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not know how -- he has already discussed so many kinds of mistreatment that I am trying to draw his attention to something in particular without suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are. Ask him the type of mistreatment he observed, the types.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, besides what you have already told us about, were there other incidents of mistreatment that you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember well Landzo, called Zenga, had a small bottle filled with gasoline, and he spread it around the concrete and lit up some paper and asked Djordjic to open up his mouth. He was heating the knife on it, and then he was putting also something into his ear. He was begging, but he put it in anyway. When he took him out -- when he took out Nedjo Draganic, when Nedjo came back, he was sitting down from me. The door closed. When he returned, he showed his legs and they were burned. I remember Spasoje Miljevic --

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go back. If you remember, who was it who took Mr Draganic out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Draganic was taken out by Landzo, nicknamed Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it not appropriate to get from him the month so we can be a bit more specific, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you remember, can you remember when this incident, for instance, with Mr Draganic occurred, what month, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was also in June or maybe early July. I can't tell you the exact dates, because I really can't remember now, but I am telling you the truth. It was, as I said, in June or early July. The same day or next day the same thing happened to Spasoje Miljevic and later I saw blisters on Spasoje Miljevic's hands, but again I don't know the exact date; in June, early July.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In respect of the incident where the knife was being heated up, I believe it was with Mr Djordjic and something was put in his ear; do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object to the leading form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has mentioned the incident. We are just trying to find the approximate time when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In fact, it will be of help to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Always my goal! Sir, if I remember the incident with respect to Landzo heating up the knife and Mr Djordjic, can you approximate when that was, what month, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was all happening within a day or so, all those instances of burnings, late June, early July. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Are there other incidents of mistreatment, sir, that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember also that Landzo, nicknamed Zenga, took out Jovo Kuljanin and he brought him back with a mask and sat him down on his place, and he sat there for a long time with a mask and then he took off the mask and it was very hard for him to come to. There were many incidents, but it has been a long time and it's hard for me to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a time when the camp was visited by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In mid-August the International Red Cross arrived. There was a doctor with them. Then they removed the guards and examined the sick and gave the others the opportunity to communicate with their families, and after the ICRC left, Hazim Delic arrived with five or six other guards, and he ordered us all to face left and to sit down, and then they started beating us on the kidneys, kicking us with their boots. The guards were doing that. Then he said: "I'll give you Red Cross. This is the Red Cross for you." It lasted for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was it who said: "This is your Red Cross", sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Delic, he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Hazim Delic. He said: "This is the Red Cross for you have. I'll give you the Red Cross." He ordered the guards to beat us. They beat us and kicked us in the kidneys. They had boots on their feet. They beat all of us in the camp. Then the next day the Red Cross showed up again. We didn't want to talk to them. They were telling us: "Well, say what happened." Somebody probably did tell them what happened. They went to those in the authority and told them not to do that. Then for a while there were no beatings. Instead -- apart from some individual incidents. For instance, Nedjeljko Samoukovic and Vukasin Mrkajic, and then Vukalo, whose first name I can't recall, Dusko Bendjo, and as for us, the others, they let us alone for a while. Then after that on one occasion Hazim Delic came --

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just interrupt you for one second, if I may. Approximately how long did this while last when there were not a significant number of beatings, if you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For maybe fifteen days, something like that, around fifteen days. Then after that Hazim Delic came in. He had in his hand a shovel. He told us to face away and started beating us on our backs with the shovel. Then he made one round and then another, and then he handed the shovel to another guard. I don't recall his name, and he continued doing that. Then after that he led out Vukasin Mrkajic in front of all of us and he broke the shovel handle. He was beating him on the back and he ordered him to take off his pants and to walk around in the hangar so that we can all see what happened to him. Then they took out other people, such as Dusko Bendjo, Nenad Dragotinovic, Zoran Djordjic, and some others. They took them out and I could hear, although I couldn't see, that they were beaten. Then they were brought back in. Then after that Delic and the guards left, got out, and we all remained there. After that there were individual incidents, when people were taken out, but while I was there there were no other incidents in which all prisoners were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, were you allowed to play cards while you were in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a while. They made playing cards with the cardboard and the guards saw that. I was not involved in the games but the guards saw them and didn't do anything to them, but then Delic walked in and he asked: "Who was making the cards?" Then he started beating us, all of us. He asked Vukasin: "Who did it." Then, when he beat Vukasin with the shovel, then Vukasin picked out people who did it, and those people were taken out and beaten. I don't know whether that was allowed or not, but the guards saw that and nobody admonished anyone about that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when it was that these people were beaten for playing cards, what month or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in September.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever do any kind of work while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. We were taken out in groups and we went to unload the weapons that had been brought in to two tunnels. It was also in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the camp compound. So we went up there and unloaded those weapons in groups.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when it was that you would unload the weapons, what month, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in June and July.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went there in July, I think in early July, and the younger ones went before that, and later on there was more of it, so we went there in groups, and we even had to unload those weapons at night.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. F, how long did you remain at Celebici? When was it that you left Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Celebici on 8th October and then I was transferred to Musala. First a guard came and read out our names and said -- he said: "Sit down." Then Hazim Delic came. He read out those same names and told us to step out, and he asked us our names and whether we had fired any shots. Then he changed a couple of names and told us to sit down. Then Delic and Pavo came together. Our names were read out again and then in two groups we were taken to Musala. I was in the second group. We were driven in a Iveco van.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long did you remain at Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until 17th November, a month and eight days, nine days.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you released then when you left Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was released to the collection centre in Donje Selo, where I stayed until 1st February 1993. Then I was exchanged to Trnovo, through Igman to Trnovo. I did not spend a long time there. I just spent one night there. Then I was exchanged at Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Either at the time you left Celebici or at the time you left Musala, did you receive any kind of release document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I received a release form. It was signed by Hazim Delic. I didn't take it with me. I don't have it here, but it had his signature. My release form was signed by him.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you get the release form when you left Celebici or when you left Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Musala. After Musala we were taken back to Celebici. We spent two or three hours there until the nightfall and then Delic distributed the release forms to us. Then he took us to Donje Selo and left us there. Then I went to my wife's brother's house. There were three other families there. I have lived with them for three months.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you were at Celebici or even at Musala, were you ever charged with any offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. One second, your Honour, please. Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you agreed on the order of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We will proceed in this order. First, counsel for Mr Mucic; second, counsel for Mr Delic; third, counsel for Mr Landzo, and fourth, counsel for Mr Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Greaves, you can ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Mr F, I am going to call you by the name, Mr F. You will understand the reasons for that, will you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr F, I want to ask you, first of all, about the initial visit of police and military to your village, when you were arrested. That was at the village of Bradina, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help me about this, please: amongst the group of police officers that you recognised was a man called Zvonko Zovko. Forgive my pronunciation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina, no. I didn't even mention him. When we were arrested in Bradina I mentioned a foreign national, and I did not mention the police. Those were people who arrested us; those were people in black uniforms and camouflage uniforms. Among them there was a foreign national and among the people who I knew was Redzo Balic.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you saw Mr Zovko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not mention Zovko there. I mentioned him in the camp, not there.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Was he someone who took part in the beatings at the date of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By what my father told me, and he was about five people away from me, he said: "Why are you beating me, Zovko?" He said: "Who is Zovko?" Then he cursed his mother. That is all I know. Afterwards he beat my father. That's what he told me, and he said he would put a sock in his mouth to gag him.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: From what you were told, that police officer was someone who took part in the beatings at the gate of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: What happened at the gate, that was the worst thing that happened to you and your fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: I am sorry. Please finish answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the most -- the hardest thing that I could imagine could happen to me. I asked three times to kill me, and now that you are reminding me, I forgot to say that Gojko Miljanic was beaten there and he was taken to Number 6 and died in the arms of his son, Savo. Now you reminded me, Petko Gligorevic also died there, and it is unbelievable that one man could do that to another.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it right that the people doing the beating up at the gates were a mixed group of police and soldiers, military men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I did not know who these people were, because as soon as we were lined up against a wall, facing it, with our hands leaning against a wall. Now who beat whom -- there was a lot of them and they took turns, and they beat until the exhaustion.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Was a man called Sefko Niksic amongst those police officers at the gates of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not recognise anyone, because already in Bradina I had been beaten there, and as I came, I could not recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr F, I want to ask you now please about your knowledge of Mr Mucic. Is it right that the time when you were most aware of him was the time when releases were taking place from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first group he released, as I said. That was late June, early July. They went somewhere, and then later we found out that they went to Musala. The second group was also taken to Musala, and I was in the third group.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr F, quite a lot of the evidence that you have given to this Tribunal has been of a kind where you are uncertain about dates. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because a lot of time has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, and I mean no criticism of you. It is nearly five years, is it not, since this all happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: To be fair, would you accept that your memory as to specific dates is really not very good at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Your memory for dates concerning the incidents which happened at Celebici, your memory is not very good as to precise dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall specific dates. If I could, I would not be -- I would not have been abused as much, but we were in such fear, and we thought whether we would be taken out or not. I mean, this was my feeling. It was very difficult to remember, and now it's very difficult to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, Mr F, and I make it plain to you that I am not criticising you in any way at all for being unable to remember dates. What I want to suggest to you is that the time of the releases from the camp was, in fact, in August 1992. Would you accept that that may well be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were released to be exchanged, or when they were leaving Number 6? I did not understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Let me make it plain that it is being released either to go to Musala or being released totally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prisoners who were being released to Musala, it was first the elderly and the sick ones, and that was in late June, early July. That was the first group. The second group was, I think, late July, early August, and I was released in October, but the first group was the elderly and the sick, were late June, early July.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr F, I suggest to you that the releases were, in fact, taking place in August, and that you are mistaken about these dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all brought in, the elderly and the sick, and all of us were all brought to Number 6, and later, after a period of time, they separated out the elderly and the sick, and took them somewhere. Later we found out they went to Musala. That was in June and early July, because they were not with us any longer. Among them was my father.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr F, can I move now to the information that you had about Mr Mucic? Would you accept that you were dependent almost entirely on what other people told you for information about Mr Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to Mr Mucic, when he arrived for the first time, I did not know him, but because he stayed a longer period of time, he was walking around, he stood in front of me and asked me: "Who are you? What is your name? Where are you coming in?" Then he said: "Okay. Sit down." Later he said: "Are you all right? Are you healthy? ." Boro Gligorevic was next to him and I helped him get up. He said: "What does this one have?" We said: "Such and such." He said: "Step out." He went on and on, one by one, and then those people were moved to Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Would your Honour just give me a moment, please? Mr F, apart from that occasion when you physically saw Mr Mucic, much of your other information has come from other people; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I was told. That was Mr Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr F, amongst the prisoners who were talking about the beatings and what they should do about it, what you have told us is that they were keen to tell Mr Mucic about it or perceived him as the person to whom they could speak about the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: But were frightened to do so because the guards would find out that they had reported it and beat them again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you why they did not tell him. Those were people who knew him, who had known him from before, so they thought of asking him, but did not ask him. I don't know why. I would not dare ask him. I would not dare come over to him to ask him, and I also did not have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Was that because you were frightened that the guards would take revenge for what you had done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was afraid of everyone down there. Whoever walked in, I was afraid of them, and prayed to God not to be taken out, because I was not sure that I would come back alive if I were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: You have told us earlier that when beatings were taking place and the Commander was reported as coming, it would stop immediately; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Was that because the guards wanted to conceal from the Commander what they had been up to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. That calls for speculation. He cannot know what the guards' purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps I may be permitted to explore it as to whether he heard anything from the guards as to why they wanted to conceal it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you become aware of why it was the guards stopped beating you when the Commander came.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. The way he has phrased it again calls for speculation. If he asked him if he heard from the guards, that is a different story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He is asking "were you aware." If he heard it, that is fine. He is calling for speculation what the guards' intention was. If he heard it, that is a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I rather think if he heard it, he has become aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you ask that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you hear why it was the guards would stop beating and was it because the Commander had arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In all probability, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just return for one question, please, to the initial period of your detention and ask you about one particular person? Do you recall during the course of your detention and beatings seeing a man called Mr Vekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were detained in Number 6, five or six of them arrived and he introduced himself as Vekic. He says: "You need this, you Serbs, and you will be left with nothing, maybe a little bit of the Belgrade Pashaluk." That I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: After the Red Cross had visited in August 1992, in August generally, was there an improvement in the conditions, such as food and medicine and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to the medicine, there was nothing there except for those in number 22. I think that the doctors could explain that better, the doctors that will come. I only remember asking for a pill once for diarrhoea and I received it, and for the rest I do not know about the medicine, who they were giving them to. I remember we had dysentery at one point and so this is what we asked for at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr F. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could use the podium, it might be a lot easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You will question him for fifteen minutes and we will go for a break and come back at 11.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran, and, as I am sure you have guessed, I am one of the defence attorneys. I am going to ask you a few questions, and if you would listen to my questions, and if you have a problem understanding them, let me know and I will repeat them and rephrase them. If you just answer the questions, I think this might go a little quicker. Can we do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That will be fine. Let me start at the very end of the direct examination, the questions Ms McHenry asked you. One of the questions she asked you was whether you were ever charged with an offence; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Do you recall she asked you if you had ever been charged with an offence, with a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. She didn't ask me that, but I hadn't been charged with anything.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, you remember meeting with an investigating commission while you were in Celebici, did you not? You testified yesterday that a man asked you about whether or not you had firearms, things like that. You remember that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And that man wrote down what you said, and you signed a document for him, did you not, about the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did sign it. I did sign something, but I don't know what he wrote there, because it wasn't read out to me after I told him those things.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, and you are not disputing the fact you possessed an automatic rifle, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And you are not disputing the fact that you had that with you when you were initially arrested, initially captured, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: You are disputing that? You are disputing the fact that you had it when you were arrested, or you did have it when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the rifle when I was arrested, and I surrendered the rifle together with the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, you had two, 30-round magazines, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had two magazines with 60 bullets, and I surrendered all the ammunition that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That is true. Sir, I am not familiar with the law on possession of automatic weapons in your country. I am much more familiar with it in my own, but in my country it is a serious offence to have an automatic weapon. How about in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually your question was whether he was convicted of any offence, was it not? That is what you are driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. My notes reflect he was asked if he was charged with an offence. I am just trying to bring out he possessed an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. He has admitted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why do you not just ask him if he had a permit for that automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of permit from officials to have that automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And you are not claiming you were a soldier or anything like that, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is a cafe owner. He runs a cafe. At least, that is what I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is what I understand. Sir, let me go back to when you initially arrived at Celebici. First, you were beaten severely before you got there, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: When you got to Celebici, you were lined up against that 3-metre high wall, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: At that point the soldiers there told you: "Now you learn the Koran." Is that not what they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Those were the guards at the camp; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we got in, I also forgot to say that. They told us that we would learn the Koran now. They said things and then we repeated them. We said "Selam Aleikum Merhaba", "Praise the Lord!", and other kinds of greetings. Then we had to repeat everything after them.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Then some people came up from outside the camp. Some soldiers and police started to arrive, is that not right, from outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They kept coming from all over the place. There were many of them as we were standing lined up against the wall. I just know that they took turns and they beat us until they got tired.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Those were the people that came up in the vehicles from outside the camp. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some were already in the camp when we got there, and as for the others, there were some vehicles coming in, but I was not allowed to turn around. I was facing the wall. I couldn't turn around.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, it was the first night that you were in hangar 6 with this man -- I am going to spell the name because I will have a hard time pronouncing it -- V-E-K-I-C -- is that Vekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: It was the first night that you were in hangar 6 that he came in and introduced himself and started beating people; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember if it was the first night. Maybe the second or the third night he introduced himself as Vekic, and he said that this is what we Serbs need and the only thing we would be left with would be the Belgrade Pashaluk. He beat one or two people. I don't remember because this was at night. I just heard the moans. Maybe it was one person or two people. I just heard them scream: "Oi!, Oi!" I think it was raining and they had small flashlights in their hands and they showed those lights, and they had raincoats on.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Now, those people were from a unit in Sarajevo, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Well, did they not -- they were not associated with the camp, though, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most likely they weren't, because they never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So they appeared in the camp on one occasion and they were never seen again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think that I saw them again. There were some other people from Mostar, who came into the camp, and they went from one person to another asking: "Is there anyone here to work in Mostar?" I also remember that there was a man by the name of Miso Zuza. Miso he was a small man, maybe 40, 50 kilos. He said that he was up to it, and then they told him to do push-ups, and then he was -- he beat him in the stomach. Then later on Landzo, nicknamed Zenga, used the same method.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, was it the first night that you were in hangar 6 that they brought the people from tunnel 9 into the hangar; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was not the first night. It was after several days. I don't remember how many days, but it wasn't the first night. We were there on our own on the first night. It was several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: The people brought from tunnel 9 were pretty well beaten up when they arrived at the hangar, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, one of the people you mentioned was Mirko Kuljanin; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, his head was bandaged, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was, yes. I think. They were covered in blood and all swollen, black and blue under and above their eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: But you are not telling the judges that these people were beaten at Celebici, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were brought to Celebici. That's what I heard later. They were brought in on 26th May and I was brought in on 27th. They were taken to Number 9 and then they were -- I am sure that they went through the same thing as we did. I heard it from them that they were beaten in the Celebici camp, just as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Well, if someone were to say that these people had been severely beaten before they arrived at Celebici, you would not know whether that was right or wrong, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the occasion of their being brought in from Bradina, when they were brought in on 26th from Bradina, until the time when I saw them, it is most likely that they were beaten there en route from Bradina to the camp, until the time when I saw them. That's where they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: En route from Bradina to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and in the camp itself, in the camp itself. That's what I heard from them, that they were also beaten in the camp, and when they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: But they would know more about that than you would, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there will be witnesses who were in the first group, and that they would be able to provide more details about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is convenient to stop now. So we will break now and reassemble at 11.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You can continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Sir, are you back on the interpretation now? Can you understand me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: A couple of questions, I think, and we will be done. Sir, at some time, at some point in time while you were being held at Celebici in hangar Number 6 were beds ever brought into the hangar, maybe bunk beds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Did there come a time when people were allowed visits from their families or family members could bring them things like food and clean clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about visits, and as for the food, people started bringing food at the gate, and then the guards distributed them. The food was in the bags and there were names put on the bags, and then the food was distributed but when I myself left, I asked my wife why she didn't send me anything and she said that she did, but I received the food very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Thank you very much, your Honour. I will pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms McMurrey. It is your turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I have to change some headsets around here. May it please the court. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dobodan, Mr F. No, it is Doboutra.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's all the same. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just for clarification purposes, you have made three different statements since May of 1992, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What three statements are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. You made a statement in Celebici on June 2nd, 1992, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the first statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The second statement you gave to the prosecution on February 27th, 1996, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And the third statement you gave just a few months ago, November 14th, 1996, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about the third statement, about the date. I gave just two statements. I gave just two statements.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you are saying that Ms McHenry, Sabine Manke and an interpreter named Savic did not record a statement of yours on November 14th, 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 14th November 1996, 14th November, one, two, three -- one was in Konjic, that is in Celebici. The second one was in 1996. Then you said in which month of -- yes, yes, that is correct. Three statements.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Mr F, I was wondering, you have never looked over here. Do you think you could maybe look at us when you are testifying, because I am going to be asking you questions and so you are going to be talking to me. I don't know if that is possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a few questions here. Number one: the Prosecutor called you and told you that we would like to have an opportunity to talk to you also, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You refused to allow us to discuss the case with you until today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That you talk to me? Well, I was called the first time and now I am talking to you. I haven't had an opportunity to talk to you before.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the prosecution did not tell you that we wanted an opportunity to visit with you ahead of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no need for that, nor did they tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may clarify, we have made it clear both in court and in proceedings with respect to some witnesses we go through a representative. In fact, we do not ourselves have even the contact information, and that is why with respect to our Pleadings and in our representation we indicate that representations have been made to us either by the witnesses or their representatives. So I believe that this may be a reason for this confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now if you had actually listened and relied on his answers, he said there was no need for that. He said so. So I do not see why you need bother.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am trying to make a record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He indicated there was no need for speaking to you. He said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am just trying to get it on the record of this trial that we have made an effort --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Everything he says will be on record, not only what you say, what he says too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May I clarify the question as to how Ms McHenry explained it to me, so maybe he can respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not part of the proceedings. Ask him the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is cross-examination and I have a right to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not cross-examining Ms McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, I am cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Go ahead and ask him the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr F, you did not allow the defence the same courtesy as you did the prosecution as far as having advance interview with you, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is your opinion; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You listed your employment as unemployed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for the time being, yes, temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you have been unemployed since May of 1992, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object as to relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will respond. Where he is getting paid during this period of time is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask him -- you go ahead and respond. I am not familiar with this type of behaviour. If you ask a question, you expect an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I would like to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Then you listen and get the answers before you get on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know. The jurisdictions in which you practise, you behave differently, but I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask your question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. You have been unemployed since May of 1992, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you have been subsidised and how you have been living since that date, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the jobs that I could do, I did not shirk any kind of a job in order to get some money to be able to support myself and my family, and if some had thought about that before, then I would still have my old job and I would be my own master. Everything I had was burnt -- not even the hen house is there -- and now I have been forced to go from one relative to another and do all kinds of most difficult jobs in order to survive and to support my family.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr F, you were a waiter before, were you not, and this is a fairly common job, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you are saying that you are living with your relatives; nobody else is making payments to you to live during this period, are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I am telling you I do all kinds of jobs that I am able to do, wherever they may be, regardless of what kind of a job it is, in order to survive and support my family.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Other than what you make are you being subsidised by the Commission for Serbs in Belgrade or some other form? That is what I am asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have worked and managed to support my children, and if you mean my coming here, we received some assistance from an association of the detainees, that is correct, yes, former prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I thank you. I am not talking about your travel here. I know that is supposed to be paid for by the Tribunal. I am asking you: between 1992 and today has another organisation subsidised your living expenses other than what you were able to earn to support your family?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that this is improper and really an affront to his dignity. If the defence counsel wants to ask whether or not he is getting paid in exchange for his cooperation with the Tribunal or something, I have no objection to such a direct question, but bringing out the fact that these people are maybe refugees -- I mean, I do not know the exact answer to this, but I think it is unfair to put the witness through this. If she has a direct question about whether or not his cooperation has resulted in him getting money that he would not otherwise have received, I do not object to that question, but in general I object to the whole line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question has nothing to do with his testimony here in the Tribunal. It has to do with the motive for fabrication. If he is being paid by the SDS or if he is being subsidised by the Belgrade Commission for Serbs, then there is a motive there that could taint his testimony somewhat. That is why I am asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Put the question to him directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I do not know how to ask it any more directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You have already formulated it. You have mentioned the organisations which are likely to do so. Ask him those questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr F, have you been paid money as living expenses during this period other than what you have earned and other than what the Tribunal has provided for you to come here, to take part in this proceeding, by any other Serbian organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I am speaking the truth and nothing but the truth. I did not receive anything from any organisation, nor is there an organisation such as this. We were called by the Association of Prisoners to come here and to speak the truth before this Tribunal, and I did not receive any money for that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is exactly what I was asking. Thank you. I wanted to ask: you were born in Bosnia, were you not -- I am sorry -- Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In what village were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: As such, you are really a Bosnian Serb, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb, yes, I am a Serb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you are also a Bosnian Serb, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Bosnia, but I am Serb by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, in the referendum of March 1st, 1992 you had the opportunity to vote and you could have voted if you had wanted to in that referendum, could you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did vote.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are an -- in 1992 you were an active member of the SDS, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992 I was a member of the SDS, yes. From January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe you have stated that you were armed during 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also stated that on May 25th 1992 a military action began against the town of Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 25th May we came under attack from Muslim and Croatian coalition. It was a sudden attack and immediately on 26th May the men from the village of Donje Bradina were killed, as I learned later, and everything was burnt. By 27th only a few of the houses were left standing, that had not been burnt by then.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were captured in May of 1992, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested in May, yes, on 27th May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually the question is: you were captured. That is the question; not: you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested, yes. I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you were arrested, you had an automatic weapon with ammunition in your possession, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was arrested, I had with me a rifle and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you also stated, I believe, to Ms McHenry yesterday that you had purchased that rifle in the parking lot of the restaurant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And you had purchased it some time in December of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You stated that there were growing tensions around December of 1991, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Those growing tensions in 1991 were directly related to the speech that your leader, Radovan Karadzic, had made on October 14th 1991 in the Sarajevo Assembly, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The reason why I did that was because the media had reported that in 1991 the HOS and SDA were already formed, and there were attacks on the army, and since my village had at the time, according to the 1991 census, 602 or 604 inhabitants, and we were surrounded by Muslim villages, there was a fear in me that my house would be attacked. So the only reason why I took the weapon was to protect my house, my child, and my family.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to leave the military discussion to another person, who is much more knowledgeable than I am about this, but you did state that there was no resistance in Bradina. Is that not what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no resistance at all. If there had been any resistance, then the people would not have been captured and taken to the Celebici camp on 26th May already.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: There were many forces, combined forces, there in the attack at Bradina, were there not? The HVO, the TO and the MUP, the military police, were all participating in this, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bradina was attacked by HOS, and they had the assistance of our Muslim neighbours and Croats that lived around us.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: What you are saying is that with all of these forces attacking Bradina, it took them three days to capture you and to liberate this town. Is that not what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I am concerned, since I was on the opposite side of Bradina at the exit towards Sarajevo, on 26th in the morning they had already burnt Lower Bradina. It was already on fire. On 26th in the evening I went to the larger village of Barakusa, because my village had only eight houses. We spent the night there, and then in the morning at around 8.00 or 9.00 am we were arrested there. I surrendered my weapon and then we were taken further on.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You told Ms McHenry yesterday that when you surrendered your weapon, you turned over your weapon and 45 bullets and that your gun had not been fired. Is that not what you told her yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I surrendered my weapon and 60 bullets. I had not fired a single bullet. This foreign national on the occasion of my arrest, he verified that and he noted down the first name and last name together with all the others who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The truth is in your statement on June 2nd, 1992 you stated that you had 270 rounds and that you had fired your weapon that day, when the fighting started, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true. I did not say that. I said the same thing down there. I said that I did not fire a single bullet, and as for what they wrote there, I don't know about that. I signed something but I don't know what it was that I signed. I did not state this.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I am going to leave that line of questioning also. The day that you were arrested from Upper Bradina and taken to Celebici, it is true that the worst torture of you, other than the fact that you saw your father being beaten, was from the time you were arrested in Bradina until the time you got to Celebici, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already answered that question earlier. Why do you want it again?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I guess I maybe was not paying attention earlier. If we have that on the record, then I accept that. Thank you. Now you also said, when you were arrested, after your initiation at the front gate, you said you did not see and could not identify any of the guards. Is that not what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I was facing the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also have stated that not only were Croatian soldiers, military police, the guards and civilians present; civilians were also coming in to participate in this beating of the new prisoners from Upper Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. This has been asked and answered both on direct and on prior cross-examination. He has stated on numerous times that he was facing the wall and he doesn't know exactly where those people were from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe he did state there were some civilians coming in. I wanted to clarify it was not just military action. There were civilians being brought in at the time also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually if you want him to say again what he answered in respect of questions by other counsel, you can repeat as many of them as you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr F, there were also civilians that participated in the beating that night on May 27th, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27th May 1992, on that night I did not say that. I did not say that for that night. When we were brought in Number 6, I did not say that. I just said that Vekic and his men came and he introduced himself, and I already said what he had said to us.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry. I maybe did not make my question clear. I am talking about the beating against the 3-metre wall at the gate of Celebici camp. You stated that there were civilians that participated in that beating, did you not, when you arrived at 1.00 pm in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, if he said they were all facing the wall and did not look back, I do not know whether he could have seen civilians or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he knows. If he does not know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How could he from behind? Has he eyes from behind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he would know who is beating him and who is beating the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am just asking him, if he knows, did he notice that civilians came?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If they were among those who were beating him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were civilians among the people that beat the prisoners at the entrance gate to Celebici camp on May 27th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I have to tell you that I was facing the wall. I don't know how many and who it was, but they beat us as much as they could, as much as they wanted. We stood there until nightfall, because when we came to Number 6, they put the lights on, and it was about 7.00 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let me ask you: the person you said beat your father, the one person you did recognise, I believe his name was Zvonko Zovko, and I apologise for my pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to object. This was gone into with last defence counsel. He said this is what happened to his father. I do not think it is fair to have the exact same question put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not the same question. That man was a Croatian, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said you were taken to Hangar Number 6, but I want to go back a little bit. You said there was one person. I think his name was Miro Vujcic, who was shot trying to escape; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That was the afternoon of May 27th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 27th May. He stood to my left and when he saw what I had been through, the torture, in order to end his own suffering, he couldn't bear it any more, and he had been beaten before, he started to run. I don't know how far, because I had been beaten myself and I heard the burst of fire and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You witnessed that also, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also stated, I believe, on your testimony yesterday that when you went to hangar 6 you were the first people brought into hangar 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you were not the first prisoners brought to Celebici, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 26th, the first ones were brought, but they were taken to Number 9. I only heard of that later, when they came over to us.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The other towns that were liberated before Bradina were Bjelovcina, Cerici and Donje Selo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: They were already at Celebici, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as I heard in number 22, this is what I heard but did not see.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr F, I just wanted to ask you: I want to make an agreement with you. I will question you a lot shorter and we will get this over with a lot faster if we are clear. The questions I am asking you, I only want you to tell me what you personally know and what you have personally seen or heard. What other people have told you is another question. I want to find out what your knowledge is in this case. So if you answer me directly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: -- then I will be finished before lunch and so will you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now you also stated in Hangar Number 6 that they turned the lights on. Is that not what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At our arrival, yes. That was on 27th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you are saying that there was electricity in Hangar Number 6 on May 27th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I hope you will forgive me with my pronunciation of these Bosnian names, because they are very alien to me but you did testify that someone named Pero Mrkajic was thrown into Hangar Number 6 and you saw him badly injured; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a while -- we had been there two or three days -- a group was brought in that had been captured. I heard later it was at Igman --

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Remember this about what you heard later. I am just asking you about what you saw and what you personally experienced. If we can leave it to that, then this will be very short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Pero Mrkajic was among them and at night he came and he dropped right on my feet and feet of Pero Gligorevic. We pushed him away from us. We didn't know who he was. Somebody at the door said: "Where is Pero Mrkajic? Curse his mother." Somebody else said: "He's had enough." After the door closed we asked him who was he, and he barely was able to say "Pero", and I could barely recognise him, because I knew him for so many years.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: He was in very bad condition at that time; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the dawn broke, he was in no shape at all. He couldn't eat. He just took a small drink of water. He was there for about a week and then was transferred to number 22, and later there he died, which is what the doctors who were present there will testify to.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I am still asking you about your personal knowledge. You saw his injuries, but you personally do not know where or who or the circumstances behind how he was beaten, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was before the arrival into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also stated that the guards never came into the hangar at night and during the day they only came into the hangar in twos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At night they would not enter into the hangar. They would just come to the door and call out from there, and people had to come out as they were called out. During the day they would come in, two of them, at a time. One would stand at the door and the other one would go around, or if he beat people, he would beat them, or he would call people to come out.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, what I want to find out here is: you have testified to Ms McHenry about a lot of people that were beaten and then died from their injuries, etc. Now, most of these people, other than a very few of them, were beaten outside the hangar, and you were not able to go outside the hangar and witness who or what or the circumstances of these beatings, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I could not see, but you could hear. You could hear their wails and their screams.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You mentioned a Mr Jovanovic and you specifically stated yesterday you recognised the distinctive voice of Esad Landzo, but you did not see anything about the beating and you did not see who hit him. You just heard Mr Landzo's voice. Is that not your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard the voice, because his voice is distinctive. It's a characteristic voice. When he was speaking outside, we knew immediately that he was coming, and we already were in fear, because his voice is high-pitched.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: My question is that you still did not view the beating, so you do not really know who hit or the circumstances of the beating of Mr Jovanovic, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who beat him. I did not say who beat him. I just said who called him out and this was all outside.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now you also stated yesterday in your examination and in your examination today by Ms McHenry that the guards followed Mr Delic's orders, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
