utterances.text: You each used an example of the military police, that Mr Delic ordered Mr Landzo and the other guards to beat the people from Bradina for breakfast, lunch and dinner. Was that not your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He ordered the guards; that is he ordered to Landzo. I did not mention the police. He ordered Landzo when he was there, coming in after him, he said: "Zenga, from today on this is their breakfast, lunch and dinner."

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you did state also today that Mr Landzo carried out the orders of Mr Delic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did it on his own as well, even when Delic was not around.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But when Delic was not around, you do not know that Mr Delic did not order him to do that ahead of time, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions on your other statement. You have never described Mr Landzo. You described a few other people in your statement, but you never described Mr Landzo. Mr Landzo was about 18 years old at the time, was he not, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how old he was, but he behaved as if he was older. I described yesterday how Landzo appeared. I described him last night.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. I am just saying in your other statement you never described him and I am just asking: you left out his age in 1992. He was very young at the time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how old he was, but he looked to me serious and also he looked terrible to me, because he beat -- I don't know how old he was and I was not enquiring then but I know that we were all afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you saw Mr Landzo in the presence of Mr Delic, you could tell that Mr Delic had control and extreme influence over Mr Landzo, could you not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. This calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am asking what he saw. If he saw that, then he is able to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is opinion, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he saw that, yes. You can tell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do not ask him his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise the control that Mr Delic had over Mr Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Same objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He is his superior. I think he is testifying as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Who said so?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. That will be my next question. Mr Delic was Mr Landzo's superior, was he not, in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We object. Calls for speculation, unless he has some personal knowledge of the chain of command in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But I think he has said already something on this, that orders were obeyed. I think in direct examination the question was put to him. Mr Delic was treated as a sort of a commander in the sense that the other guards obeyed him. I think this is a question which has already come on the record. I do not think that Ms McMurrey has to have it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am asking again: could you recognise the relationship between Mr Delic and Mr Landzo? Was it one of control?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Same objection, your Honour. Calls for speculation and opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually this witness is not in a position to tell you what the relationship is. Find someone else to do that, not him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, may I ask him to describe how Mr Landzo acted at Mr Delic's orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is suggesting that Mr Delic is giving him orders. That is what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has already testified that he responded to the orders of Mr Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think something did come in the direct on this relationship between Delic. Can we have that particular passage?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have it written down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us get your questions. If all you are asking is the structure, I am not sure this witness is the right person to tell you the structure in that organisation. He is not the right person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think something has already come on the draft transcript. Ms McHenry is checking up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday the draft transcript reveals at least on one occasion -- I do not know about other things -- that the witness reported with respect to Hazim Delic: "He came and said: 'What are you guys doing up there? They are killing our police officers.' He cursed our mother. Then he started beating people one by one and he ordered Zenga: 'This is what the people from Bradina are to get for breakfast, lunch and dinner', and from that day on we did not receive any dinner."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If you read further, it says Landzo carried out his orders, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness in his answers confirmed that Landzo could do it even without being ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he is testifying to what Mr Landzo does, I have a right to know whether he did it under orders, your Honour. That is what I am asking him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not through him. He would not know who gave him orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he was present, he would, and if he can testify that he did not know whether he was ordered at other times, then that raises the issue that he was probably acting under orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think he is obliged to answer even this question. He is not obliged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I do not know what I am allowed to question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, you also asked him questions about the position of Delic in the camp, if I remember correctly. He did say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I believe that came up the first thing this morning, and he certainly said that he understood that Delic was -- I do not want to say the exact -- I can possibly find it in the transcript from early this morning but I do not have it from yesterday. Thank you. I will look it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, I will rephrase the question, where it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are trying to complicate the position between the accused persons. Now when a person is giving evidence, you ask him questions within the scope of his knowledge. You do not go about asking people questions which are not within the scope of their knowledge. Even whatever he says is a matter of guesswork.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In our motion for separate trial, we told you there would be inconsistent defences in this case and there are inconsistent defences. I am not trying to raise problems with the court or the other defence attorneys. I am trying to represent my client to the best of my ability. That is what I am here to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I have told you from the beginning perhaps your ability might be more detrimental to him. Ask him the questions. Ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr F, when Mr Delic ordered Mr Landzo to carry out orders, can you tell me what his demeanour was, Mr Landzo's demeanour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo both on orders of Delic, on his own did things that a regular person would never think about. For instance, when he tied a cord around Vukasin Mrkajic, and then when he had the other one run around the hangar, when he took people out and inside Number 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He is answering the question which he was asked. Let him answer the question. Say as much as you know about what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, to do push-ups, to hit him in the abdominal area, that is what he did. Maybe nobody even knew about these things. Other things he did on orders, which is what I already stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My next question to you is even when Mr Landzo was carrying out things in -- outside the presence of Mr Delic, you do not know that they -- whether he was acting under orders or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about -- you had mentioned a Nenad Cecez and a Davor Bendjo, I believe, in your earlier testimony. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Those were prisoners with you in hangar 6, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They distributed food to us and brought it, and they were outside of the hangar. That is one was inside, one was outside, and when we were to go to urinate, they were at one time given instructions that they could take people one by one to go and do that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, they were really considered the organisers of the prisoners, and any communication you had with the guards, you would tell these people and they would inform the guards; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what they were, but they were among us, and we needed to go to them if we wanted to go to the toilet, urinate and other things.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, their duties really started at 6.00 am in the morning until after dark and after dark they were allowed outside the hangar, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not allowed out.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to the -- you had testified earlier about two brothers who were brought to the camp, (REDACTED) is that correct? I am very sorry. Can we -- I did not ask any questions about what they were referring to. I will come back to that. You have testified about a lot of different tortures, and I know that Ms McHenry had said that her goal was to help me clarify all this, and I appreciate that. When you testified about Spasoje Miljanic and Nedeljko Draganic, you told us about some injuries that they sustained, but the truth is that you were not outside the hangar and you did not witness what actually happened to these people, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not Spasoje Miljanic. It was Spasoje Viljavic and Nedjo Draganic. I was not outside and I did not even state that. I was in Number 6 when they returned. Their trousers were seared through. I saw on Draganic's legs and he shouted to us and Spasoje Miljanic after a while -- at first he was silent and later he showed us his hands and we saw -- I saw blisters -- burns on his palms.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now you also testified, I believe, that -- I may need to ask how to refer to certain things, and I do not know how to refer to it, but you testified that there were some people who were forced to do some sexual acts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, those people were not brought to Celebici until after the murder of the military police on July 12th, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, their being brought to Celebici was in connection to the murder of the military police, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. That's not how I stated it. They were brought in -- I don't know why they were brought in, and again I must say that this is what I heard. You told me not to say what I have heard but this is what I heard. They were brought to Number 6, and every morning Zenga beat them, and after all that, he ordered them to get up in front of all of us and one of them put out the sexual organ and put it into the other's mouth, and then they switched. One was made to kneel and do it. We could all see this, because this is what happened in Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: My question is: this all happened after 2th July 1992, did it not, after the death of the military police? I believe you already answered "yes", if I am correct? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall, but I know they were brought in after us, most probably after that. If you will allow me, I can tell you I do not know that, but from that village there were some women the same last name, and Balic Redzo was killed there at that time, and later it turned out that those policemen were killed by the Muslims from Repovci, if you really want to know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: At the time when the incident occurred, since nobody really knows what happened to the military police, the TO and the people from Celebici were told that the Serbians had killed the military police, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, she has already -- at one point she frequently tells the witness not to answer things he cannot know himself. At other points she asks things that it is clearly obvious he would have no way of knowing. I must object.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, all he has to say is he does not know. If he does not know, then I will move on to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are doing the answering for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry. I was responding.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, not with respect to any of the recent testimony, previously with respect to some testimony we would like to formally request a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I agree. There is no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What is your next line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I am not finished with this line of questioning. If he knows, I am asking him: that day of July 12th, Mr Landzo went to the scene where the military police were killed, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. You also testified, when the attorney for Mr Mucic was cross-examining you, that there was an outbreak of dysentery and that you asked for medication and you received it, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also testified when the attorney for Mr Delic was questioning you that early on in May of 27th -- I don't remember the name because it doesn't show up here -- someone named Poso Miljevic was forced to do push-ups and he was killed, I believe -- I am not sure what your testimony was. You also stated that Mr Landzo used the same method later, not in May; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can repeat that for you. When they came, and these persons --

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just tell us who they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- were unknown to us, the unknown persons from Mostar, they entered Number 6 and they asked whether there was somebody there who was from Mostar. The little Zuza answered, and then he said: "Okay. Now do push-ups." He hit him -- actually he kicked him in the abdominal area and then later that same method was used by Landzo on other inmates who were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, that question that night by the Mostar Croatian forces, who were those were that came in, that question was designed to find out who in the building was a JNA reserve soldier, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that the Croats were coming. I said they were unknown persons. They came and they did what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have Prosecution Exhibit number 1, I believe, which is the drawing of the inside of Hangar Number 6, so that we can put it on the ELMO, and I would like to ask Mr F to show us exactly where he was sitting, please. First I would like to ask you: does this look like an accurate representation of Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is. This is the entrance. This is how you get in, and I sat right here in the middle, facing the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I would like the record to reflect that he pointed at the back left-hand wall, since I do not have a drawing to introduce into evidence. Thank you. Also I would like to ask you a couple of questions about Hangar Number 6. You already identified the one door. That was the only door that was used for Hangar Number 6, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was the door that was used for entering the hangar. There were other doors that could be opened, but they were never opened until the arrival of the International Red Cross. You could get in with a truck. This was the large door and that door was opened twice after the arrival of the Red Cross. Then they were again opened when it was called, but the entrance door, this door was used most of the times.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The side where those big hangar doors were, when they were closed, there were no holes you could look out of, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't look.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: There were windows in the hangar that were about 3 metres up, where nobody could see out; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how high they were, but I know they were quite high. They were on the upper side and nobody could do anything about them. I think there were also small windows above the door or maybe not. I know that there were doors on the upper parts and there was a door on the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But the only door that was ever used was the one that you indicated on the drawing that you were just shown; is that correct, except when the Red Cross was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: -- sitting against the outside wall of this hangar. Is it not true that the hangar was sealed on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: There was no way for you to stick your hand out or get air or anything from the bottom, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Water. I know that when it was hot, I don't know who it was of the guards, I can't remember, he sprayed water on the roof and also down there where people were sitting, and they were not allowed to get up. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you are saying there was maybe enough -- it was not sealed enough to prevent rain water or water from dripping in. Is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The water could get in, but only when it was sprayed in through a hose, and the rain water fell on the roof. I could tell you that I didn't really have an opportunity, nor did I dare to look. When I was leaving the hangar, I did that with my head down. When I was going to the hole that had been dug up for our toilets, and I went back to the hangar with my head down.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, my question is: you could not stick your hand out at the bottom of the hangar, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't try to do that. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That brings me to the toilets. There were holes dug. As you came out the door and you were facing Hangar Number 6, to the right-hand side towards the back there was something, a makeshift toilet of some sort, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right-hand side? On the right-hand side there was a machine gun nest and then at the exit of the hangar there was also a machine gun nest on the hill, and behind the hangar, maybe five steps to the right of that hill, there was first one hole, the second hole, the third hole and so on. When they would fill up, we would cover them and dig new ones. It was not on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. There were only two guards guarding about 240 prisoners in each shift; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were more of them. I don't know how many of them were outside, but there were two machine gun nests, one to the right of the entrance and one on that hill at the entrance. In fact, to the right of the entrance door and then opposite of the tarmac, opposite the entrance there was a machine gun nest.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: As far as the guards that were on duty guarding Hangar Number 6, you only saw two at a time, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to ask you about this person named Zjelko Klimenta. You know that he was killed by a gunshot wound, but you know that that was an accidental shooting, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The guard was crying after that happened, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The statement you made -- you testified today that you saw Mr Landzo in August or September at Celebici with a white belt on; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That white belt represents a member of the military police, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most likely.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe you stated that he came to talk to Dusan Bendzo; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: They had a conversation outside of the hangar, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you did not personally hear what the conversation was about, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Landzo could have been a member of the military police even earlier than August, could he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. He would probably have worn the white belt.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you made a statement in November that Mr Landzo was in Celebici camp all the way through October, did you not, and that was not correct, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say in November. I said that some time in late August and early September -- I don't know exactly when -- that he left the hangar, in fact, Number 6, and that then he would be seen from time to time wearing a white belt, and that he called out Dusko Bendjo.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also stated in your written statement to Ms McHenry on November 14th -- and this is the translation; it is not in your language -- you stated: "I am sure that Zenga was in the camp until I was transferred to Musala, which I believe to have taken place at the beginning of November 1992." Is that not what you testified to before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: November? I left in October. I left Number 6 in October, but he was seen, that's what I stated. He was seen while I was there. People could see him. He came there and he visited the camp, but he had a white belt at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So what you are telling us is that the statement that was given on November 14th is incorrect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has not said that. There is nothing incorrect about it. I object to her putting words in his mouth. The statement as she read it says: "I am sure he was in the camp." He has just stated that he was in the camp. I object to her suggesting that there is inconsistencies when there are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms McHenry is omitting the part where it says: "I am sure he was in the camp until I was transferred at the beginning of November". That is what I am trying to make clear here. Now the witness is saying that is incorrect. If the statement is incorrect from November 14th, I have a right to ask him to state that for the record. That statement was incorrect, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That statement is correct. I repeat again: I saw Landzo on several occasions. I don't know if he had gone away from the camp or that he was there, but that we could only see him more seldom, and he had a white belt. I don't know when he went and to where he went to, but I know that he took Dusko Bendjo out several times. I don't know what else do you want me to tell you. He was there. I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You testified that you saw him in August and September. Now he could have had the white belt and been with the military police earlier than that, could he not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will now rise and we will come back and reassemble at 2.30 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: -- for cross-examination to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We are back from lunch now. Ms McMurrey is still cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before you do that, I have a question to ask from the witness. You have shown us the place in the hall -- in this hangar where you were present. Where were the two brothers who were forced to commit those obnoxious acts? Where were they sitting in this hangar? You have got the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the opposite side, facing near the entrance door, to the right of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you could indicate the place, please, on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where they sat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is by the door, is it? They sat by the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now how were the acts done? They were called out from where they were sitting or they still remained where they were sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They got up from the place where they were sitting and they did it in front of all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The names of the brothers have been excised from the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and I do apologise to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. We knew it was a slip. It was not intentional.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Witness F, Mr F, I wanted to ask you back. The rifle that you described you bought, you bought that rifle in front of your restaurant or the restaurant Zjelko that you worked in in Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the restaurant Zjelko where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The people you brought it from were SDS Serbs, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. These persons were not known to me. When I asked them who did I buy it from, and they said: "This is not something you should be asking. If you want to buy it, buy it. If you don't want to, don't do it."

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go to a person -- you did know a man named Gojko Miljanic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr Miljanic was an older man born in about 1931, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr Miljanic died approximately on May 27th, 1992, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was beaten on 27th May 1992, and then he was brought in later into the Number 6, and he lay there to the left of the entrance, and he was showing some sign of life for maybe 12 hours, maybe a bit longer, and he died there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So he died some time way before 1st June then, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And this Mr Miljanic, he was from Bradina, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, the whole time that you were at Celebici, there was no other person with the last name Miljanic that died there, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know of any other person.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned a lot of incidents in your testimony yesterday and today, and the only names of any guards that you mentioned during this exercise were, of course, Esad Landzo and Mr Delic. You omitted to mention the other guards that you knew participated, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time. I don't remember them -- I remember them very well, because Landzo and Delic were getting inside the hangar most frequently. I know a dark man with fingerless gloves. He also took people out and beat them. There was a guy by the name of Forjak. I don't know his name. I don't know who beat people, of all those guards, and I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you did know the names at one time, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew their nicknames and for some of them I knew their names too.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In your testimony you also have described how after the Red Cross came to Celebici for about fifteen days there were not many beatings. The Red Cross came approximately on August 12th, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Red Cross came in mid-August. I think it was on 12th August; that is right, yes, on 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, after about fifteen days you said everybody was beaten again, did you not, and that includes you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also know that Esad Landzo was not present after the Red Cross visit in Celebici, was he; not as a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there as a guard after the visit of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your testimony yesterday was that you had been beaten once before, and then you had been beaten by Mr Landzo a second time -- another time. You were only beaten by Mr Landzo once. Your testimony yesterday was that he kicked you a couple of times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he kicked me. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I stated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That was before August 12th, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was when the Red Cross came. That's when those people were killed, the police officers. It was after that. It was after that. That's when he kicked me twice; two or three times he kicked me in my shin.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, that's the only time that you testify that Mr Landzo beat you personally, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. I think it was the only time.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your Honours, I have some new notes that have been passed to me. May I just have one moment? (Pause). I have one more question. As far as Mr Landzo's presence in the camp, you never saw Mr Landzo in Celebici before the end of June, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, you did not see him in Celebici when you first got there, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He showed up after our arrival there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I pass the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms Residovic, I think. You can now take over the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon to you, sir. My name is Edina Residovic. I am the defence counsel for Mr Zejnil Delalic. Mr F, you have answered a number of questions so far, the questions asked by my colleagues. I will try not to repeat what you have already been talking about. However, Mr F, the two of us, we share a problem, and our colleagues did not have that problem when they talked to you. We understand each other and we could -- I could actually ask you questions, you could answer very fast, but the judges and all the others present here would then not be able to follow our exchange. So I would like to ask you, and we have been asked to do so by the Tribunal, if after my question you could wait for this question to be interpreted and then after you give me your answer, I will again wait for a while so that everybody is able to understand what we are talking about. I think that we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have already confirmed that you gave a statement in addition to the one that you gave in Celebici in February 1996 to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You speak before this Trial Chamber of many events. You were probably shaken by your memory of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I think that you will agree that your memory in February 1996 was maybe a bit more fresh than your memory right now, today. I will, therefore, repeat some questions just to get clarification and I would appreciate if you could answer those questions as briefly as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you testified that you lived in the village of Krc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified also that you had been arrested in the hamlet of Barakusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So from the beginning of the fighting in Bradina you left your village and you were moving towards some other places; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how far apart is Barakusa from Krc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1 km, maybe a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us was it in Barakusa when you were arrested that you surrendered the weapon that you had in your possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it is true that you left your house with the weapon that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr F, could you please confirm that it is true that in your testimony you also stated that on 25th May, that on that day some groups separated and tried to cross over to the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that some of these groups were those that were arrested later on in Igman and in the -- around the village of Ljuta and were brought to Celebici when Pero Mrkajic was brought there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which one was the one that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is one of those groups that had separated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who attempted to cross over to the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was not clear to me, because I know that you testified that some groups had set off on 25th and that you did not join those groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So we are in agreement about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 26th some groups started. Maybe some did on 25th already, but I know about the morning of 26th, that some groups left.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Pero Mrkajic was in one of those groups; Zara Mrkajic was there, Djordjic and the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is what you heard. All right. Thank you very much. Is it correct, Mr F, that you testified that you were attacked from the direction of Repovci by HOS and HVO special forces and by the units from Buturovi Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said we were attached by the HOS units, who were joined by our neighbours from the village -- living around us, and they attacked Bradina, joining the forces from Buturovic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also confirmed that some of them had camouflage uniforms, that some had black shirts and trousers, and that those with black shirts and trousers had black hats too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, hats.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would also like you to confirm whether it is true that in Dragan Subotic's house that you were lined up and searched, that money, documents and similar objects were taken from you. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of Miso Kuljanin's cafe and women from in front of Subotic's house. The houses are adjoining and maybe they are 10 metres apart from one another. We were in front of Miso Kuljanin's cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony given on February 23rd, 1996, when you were speaking about these events, you said the following, that among the people who were watching the search, you recognised Zvonko Zovko among others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I mentioned that in relationship to the fact when he was beating my father.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will go back to that, Mr F. I am now referring to the events in the village of Bradina. I have your statement here and I wish to clarify this matter. In this statement you said that among the people who were present there you recognised Zvonko Zovko, your neighbour from Podorasac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of Miso's cafe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in front of Miso's cafe you recognised your neighbour from Podorasac, Mr Zvonko Zovko, and since this fact was a bit unclear, thank you for the clarification. Also in your statement you said that you recognised a man by the name of Bosnak, whose first name you do not know. Is that Zladko Bosnak from the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know his name. He was a policeman. He used to be a policemen. I don't know his name. He used to be a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: His name is Bosnak. It is not a designation of his nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what he was called. I don't know if that was his real name or his given name, but he used to be in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr F. For further clarification, taking into account a number of events and your condition even here today as a witness, I would like to ask you to remember once again for additional clarification the events surrounding your father. In your testimony so far, not before this Trial Chamber but to the Prosecutor, you said your father was three rows away -- apologies -- he was the third person away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fifth or sixth. He was down the line from me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was so close to you that you could see every word that he said and every moan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard him moan, but I could not hear every word he said.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, taking into account the small discrepancies, I would not like to confront you now, but so much time has passed. So please can you confirm that you heard on that occasion that your father said: "Don't do that Zvonko. We know each other." Then Zvonko said: "Who knows you? Fuck his mother", and he then put a sock inside his mouth to gag him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr F, you have already said quite a lot about your knowledge regarding Gojko Miljanic and Petko Gligorevic. I would just like to ask you on that day together with you from Bradina to Celebici were Petko Gligorevic and Gojko Miljanic brought there with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Gojko Miljanic died the next morning or during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Petko Gligorevic also died as soon as he arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the beating he remained by the wall and he stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it is clear that they were not with you in Hangar Number 6 after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They died immediately after that or several hours later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please allow me to go back to some other issues. Your Honours, just a moment. These were just some clarification issues. You testified that the next day after your arrival the seriously wounded people were all called out and taken to the 3rd March school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't the next day. It was within several days. I don't know exactly how many days, but they were taken there and later I heard that it was in the 3rd March school.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that these persons were given some kind of medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was released, I heard that they were given some pills, but I don't know. I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your father was also taken to the 3rd March school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your father was kept there for a while for treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your father never went back to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did return and he gave a statement in Celebici, and later he again went to Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After his statement he was not detained in Celebici any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was -- I don't know how many days he was. I can't recall that exactly, but he was -- maybe after being released -- after being released from 3rd March I think he was there for a few days, and then he returned to Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr F, you were also called after a couple of days and you gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You signed that statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated in that statement that you were a member of the SDS and that you had weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said in your statement that you were issued 270 bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that you used your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I show this statement to the witness to have him verify that it is his handwriting -- actually his signature, not his handwriting. Please could you show this to the witness and provide the Trial Chamber and everybody else with a translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are only two copies and we are three sitting here. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe I have extra ones, if defence counsel would like. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): This is the translation done by the defence, since the translation provided by the prosecutor contains several -- it was illegible in several places. So it does not contain the translation of the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask that the prosecution be given a copy of this? Let me just say in the future -- obviously it is not the prosecution who does the translation. It is the Registrar's and we have no way of knowing. So we have given the translations we have previously to the defence. If they notice there are errors, it would certainly be helpful for us if they would notify us in advance. For now I would at least please like to see a copy of the defence counsel's translation. Thank you. Mr F, do you recognise your signature on this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be my signature. I recognise that I signed it. It is my handwriting. However, what is written there, that is not the statement that I gave. The statement was not read out to me. I remember what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The defence wishes to tender this as defence exhibit. Mr F, in your testimony given to the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mark it as a defence exhibit. It will be defence Exhibit Number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is defence 1/1. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): We tender this as evidence proposed by the Delalic defence, so this is our proposal. Your Honour, do you accept this evidence, the statement given in the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This bears his signature admittedly. Whatever its value, whatever its probative force, that can be seen later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are tendering it as his statement? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): All right. Thank you very much. Mr F, can you please confirm before this court that Bradina is a village that is located on the main route M17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean M17?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Main route that's called M17. Maybe you don't know its name but it's the main route from Konjic to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that it is the only blacked-up road and the shortest road between Konjic and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please confirm that the railroad line linking Sarajevo to Ploce also goes through Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that by blocking this road the normal traffic and communication from Konjic to the places on the other side of the Ivan mountain in Sarajevo is disrupted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the roads are blocked, then also no other way to go.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that from Tarcin, and that is the first village on the other side of the Ivan mountain, to Konjic it usually takes about half an hour to travel there by car, between those two places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that if this road is blocked, the only way to go from Tarcin to Konjic is on a tarmac road through Fojnica and Djusina, and that is more than fifteen hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never went there, but I heard about that road.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr F, you know that the population of Konjic was mixed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you testify before this court that the villages and hamlets are mixed in such a manner that it is impossible to separate them without endangering the people in other villages and in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know in what way.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any way, so that each hamlet, each house, is divided. Is it not virtually impossible? I mean, we saw how it is possible by war. Everything is possible if you do it by war, but under normal circumstances is it possible to divide Konjic in such a way that people do not bother each other if you block the roads, if we do not allow each other to pass? Is the structure of Konjic such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr F, do you know that the Konjic authorities on several occasions tried to achieve a peaceful solution to the problem and to effect the surrender of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that, because if I may say this, in early April the tunnel leading towards Bradina from the direction of Sarajevo was blocked because they put the lumber and put sand in there, and on the other side they put explosives in a vehicle and by remote control the tunnel in Bradina was blown up. This is what our neighbours did. Somebody else may be a good witness to testify to that, but I only know that that night Sefko Niksic, Rale and Nusko, that's Rale Musinovic, they came. They came to Pero's cafe and they were the last ones who passed through that tunnel. That tunnel was blown up and Bradina was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you know that Bosnia-Herzegovina became independent on 6th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in April mobilisation was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you and your family -- did anyone from your family report -- answer that call-up? You would like to say something, my colleague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The TO in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the police, the police reserves, there were four people from Bradina. When they pulled out, they were by themselves: Nicon, Shojan, Seponjan, Lipoz. None of them came any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. I do not want to interrupt. Could I ask you to clarify what his answer was with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina becoming independent on 6th April. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said "yes".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He said "yes" and to the next question he said: "I don't know that either." I want to clarify there is not a translation error. If you could clarify that matter, so the record is clear? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): We can repeat this exchange. Do you know that Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state by the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that mobilisation was proclaimed in April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The next question was: did anyone from Bradina respond to the call-up and join the Territorial Defence in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You or any member of your family did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that and I don't know what mobilisation and who wanted the mobilisation. That I don't know. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yet you had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you did know something. Did you know Strahinja Zivak from Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Rajko Djordjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was one of the ringleaders, one of the organisers of the defence in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no defence in Bradina. There was no lead organiser, nor was there any defence. I think I already said that twice. On 25th May we were attacked. On 26th May people were already in the camps. The houses were burnt. Everything was destroyed. People, livestock, property -- everything around was destroyed, especially from Lower Bradina, starting on 26th, and until 27th it reached the Upper Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr F, you said now that there was no resistance. Why would 3,000 men, as you stated, take three days to capture a small village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I heard when I was released, that there were 3,000-3,500 men there. Why? You could notice that when the shooting started on 25th and the shells, if there had been any resistance in Bradina, nobody would think of that. I think that in the census of 1991 there was only 4,000 to 6,000, and I think out of that small number of Serbs and the rest Muslims and Croats, and if there were only 200 people in Bradina, what could they do against 40,000 people?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you. A little while ago when you mentioned the person by the name of Bosnak, can you please remember, since you testified about that earlier, that you witnessed when Bosnak beat Radoslav Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I was told by Radoslav. It happened at night. I asked him several days later. I said: "Who beat you so bad?", because everybody at Celebici could hardly hear me, and he said: "Bosnak".

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said something in front of this court, then you made a mistake, so it is true according to your knowledge that it was Bosnak who beat Radoslav Kuljanin. That is what you heard from Radoslav Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: do you know Ranko Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Ranko Kuljanin, no.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The security officer in the military factory in Igman in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no, I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember him that much.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: did you know that Ranko Kuljanin went by helicopter from Bradina to Belgrade at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also heard that but I don't know that. I could not -- I did not see that. I don't know where I was when I heard that, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Maybe just one or two questions. Did you in April and May go to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April, yes. That was in early April. I think I went to the office, to the administration office, to be given the vacation time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the Secretariat of the SDS for the village of Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was a member of the SDS but not of the Executive Board. I was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in April there was a decision forming the Serbian municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you did not go to Konjic in May? Do you have any knowledge of intensive shelling of Konjic in that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr F. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Madam Residovic, I just want to find out. To what force do the black uniform people belong? Any idea? I am sure of one thing. They are not lawyers. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I -- yes, they were not lawyers and not in the court room, that's for sure. I believe that some experts, military experts, will be able to explain that or other witnesses. My assumption is that the Trial Chamber will learn that in the course of the presentation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just one question in clarification. When you just testified about Mr Radoslav Kuljanin being beaten and he told you it was by a person named Bosnak, was that the only incident of beating of Mr Kuljanin that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were multiple beatings of him. As he was recovering, he sat to the left of the door about seven or eight days and then he sort of came about. Later he was beaten by Hazim Delic and on another occasion he was taken out, and I think that there will be other witnesses who may be able to tell much more about him, who may know better, but so much time has passed that I forgot a lot of things now. Some are coming back to me, but these things one forgets during all this time that has passed.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not require this witness any longer? So he could be discharged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Put down the shutters so that he can go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have been very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any other witness for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are prepared to call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This time not a protected one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will rise and come back at 4 o'clock and carry on with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can invite the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I call Mr Stevan Gligorevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let him take the oath. MR STEVAN GLIGOREVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): I am Stevan Gligorevic.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5th February 1950.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your occupation, your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am of a teacher, elementary school, first through fourth grades.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell the court where you lived at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of May 1992 I lived in Hadzici. That is one of the Sarajevo municipalitites, but I found myself in my place of birth, because I had some property which I worked in and I found myself there.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Where is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I was born, that was in Bradina. I was born in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: So by the end of May 1992 you found yourself in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: What is your ethnical background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many Serbs did live in Bradina at this time, by the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but from the census of 1991 there was approximately 602 persons living there.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: All Serbs? My question would be: were other people than Serbs living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina itself very few. There may have been three or four Croatian families and two Muslim families.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell the court what happened in the end of May in Bradina when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is what happened approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bradina was attacked from all sides somewhere around the evening of 25th May. At first there was some heavy shelling and the next day those units entered Bradina. They burnt the side from which they arrived at, which was called Suljina Strana. On that occasion, as I found out later, because I was not there at the time, approximately 20-30 people were killed. They were unarmed and at close range. My hamlet, Upper Bradina that is, those units entered the Upper Bradina the following day, which was 27th May. I was at home and I was arrested there. They collected us all in the middle of the village, which is a part called Barakusa. Some soldiers in camouflage uniforms came there and in black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr Gligorevic. Who were these units? What kind of units were they? You did not name them as far I could hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were Muslim units, I suppose, because some recognised their own classmates from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were there other than Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Probably yes. As I said, some wore camouflage uniforms and some black uniforms. Some had the chequerboards on their heads and others wore a half moon and a star.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Was there any defence against attacks on the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's hard to talk about defence, because there were village watches, like everywhere else in Bosnia at that time. There was no defence and I don't see any logic of it, because Bradina was surrounded completely, from all sides, by Muslim villages. So it stood no chance to survive as such.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you yourself do anything to defend yourself or others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you, for instance, have a weapon of some kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Have you ever been a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I should have done my military duty in 1968, but I was released because of the poor eyesight. That was to be in the former Yugoslav army. So I actually never did my national duty.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you continue your account of what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They lined us up, formed a column, and we started towards the centre of Bradina. The first collection point was midway between my village and the centre of Bradina in front of a cafe which was along the road and it was called Miso. We stood there for a while while the soldiers were taking things out of the cafe. That is they were looting it. Then in a stolen Golf car -- it belonged to a cousin of mine -- a soldier arrived and he started beating everybody. He had a long stick. I don't know. There was a pipe or something. He started beating people down to the ground. I don't know what his name was. I only know that in the end one of his superiors I guess -- I don't know who it was -- cautioned him, and he said: "Enough, Barba." I guess his nickname was "Barba." I don't know his name. Later I heard a young man, Muslim -- I heard that he was a young man Muslim from the Celebici village. After that we continued in the column towards Bradina. We were at the tunnel where the railroad tracks crossed the road, and we saw a group that was already lined up against the wall, because there is a retaining wall there, because there is a hill going up. We were lined up there as well. We had to give our personal data. Then we had to take off our shoes. We were searched. We had to turn in all the valuables that we had, rings and bracelets and everything. Then there was a truck with canopies already parked there. Then about three soldiers started calling out people.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Before you start entering the truck and telling us what happened, you said that you were giving your personal data. Was somebody questioning you, or give us some explanation as to how you were apprehended, or how should I understand this, giving your personal data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was only name, the last name and the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: So they did make a list of the people who were apprehended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many were you? Do you have any evaluation of how many people you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe -- I don't know the exact number, but 85, 86 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue the account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The procedure that followed was that one by one we would approach the back of the truck and then the order was to -- this was now early May, and Bradina is 760 metres above the sea level, so it was pretty fresh, and people had to take off everything they had, and some elderly people did not, and they beat them. Then they had to climb up into the truck. I was next to the last and behind me was Slovko Golabovic. When I stood in front of them, first I had to take off my glasses. I had to drop them on the road and then jump on them. So they broke, and I only had a twisted frame. Then I had to stand upright and the three of them started to kick me, beat me with the rifle butts, with their hands, and that lasted for several minutes. Then they told me to get onto the truck. That first time I climbed into the truck I still had some strength and I weighed at around 104 kilos. Then after my cousin Slovko was in, then they ordered me to get off again. I got off again and then the same game started with them. I had to stand upright and I got a lot of beatings, and when I wanted to climb in, I could not this time. I took a running start again, tried again. Then somebody offered me a hand from up in the truck and somehow I climbed in. Then they lowered the back of the canopy. They tied it securely. The truck was there for a while. They -- maybe the engine was not in order, because they were starting it and turning it off. Then we eventually started towards Konjic. Since the canopy was well tied up and there was sun and there was a lot of us on the truck, I was losing my breath, I was losing my air, because I was one of the last. Maybe I was in a better position, because some people were already suffocating further down. One of them, who had some health problems before, was rolling his eyes, because everybody was so packed one next to another, and was uttering some inarticulate noises. We were all drenched with sweat. After a drive we arrived at Celebici. When we entered through the gate we got out and they lined us up against a wall, which was near the gate. At that time the worst thing started. We had to stand leaning against a wall both with our chest and the stomach area, with our hands raised high. At first that was not a problem, but later for me it was more of a problem than the beatings that I received, because it is terrible, terrible pain to keep about seven hours to keep the hands up. You can't stand -- you can't do that any more, because your arms just keep sliding by themselves. Boro Koprivica was near me and his balance centre was already damaged before and he kept falling down, and myself and Slobodan Gligorevic who was on the other side of him had to help him. That was helpful because we were able to lower our arms at that time. There were three younger men in uniforms. I don't know them. I know very few people there in Konjic. They went around cursing. One of them was beating with a rifle butt. The other one with the front part, and the other one had a handle of a pickaxe, which was broken off. Then a fourth one -- I don't know if that was the same team or they took turns. One was pulling out the piece from the rifle and was beating us up with it. One of them had a large piece of stone or pebble from the river Neretva and was hitting us in the back with it. So that dragged on for hours. Some were falling and standing up again. Some people at that time were being taken out of the line-up and made to lie down and then blows were raining on them. We could not turn even for a moment to see. All this was accompanied by curses, by mocking, and I think that with all that physical torture it was also the verbal humiliation, because for a while some of the young men that were there were shouting loudly something like: "Praise the Lord!","Merhaba, Selam Aleikam!" Then we had to repeat it in unison. Then they were saying -- they were asking which religion was the best in the world. We all had to say that it was the Muslim one. Then they were saying prayers from the Koran and we had to repeat them. With all that physical torture and humiliation I also had great thirst. I was dehydrated by the hours of being in a truck coming to Bradina. After I don't know how many hours nearby there was a water pump and then one would pump and we lined up against a little canal, which was full of refuse, and since it was spring, it had all the things that fall off the trees. I saw Petko Gligorevic; I saw two streams of blood down his nose. I also saw on the ground Gojko Miljanic, who lay there motionless as well. I don't know what time it was, but I assume it was around 9 o'clock. We went to the Hangar Number 6. The lights were on. It was late May and it was nearing --

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just some more questions about what happened at this wall. You mentioned -- did I get you right? -- you mentioned the number of seven hours standing against this wall; is that correct? You stood up for seven hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly, because we came there at around 2.00 pm and we got into the hangar at around 9.00 pm. That's Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were people forced to stand with their hands up all this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. An especially bad example is my relative Radko Kuljanin, whose -- he couldn't extend his fingers, and he could not do that next to the wall, and then he was beaten with rifle butts, and Stanko Kuljanin -- he is deaf and dumb from birth -- and they would issue orders to him to keep his hands up, and he couldn't hear them, and then he would be beaten even more than the others. Also the example of Miroslav Vujcic was pretty bad. He was taken out of the line-up and to lie down on the ground. He was beaten and he couldn't go through this torture any more. He refused to go through this humiliation. He jumped up and started running. That's at least what I think, because we couldn't turn around and look what was happening. They fired some shots and killed him. When we headed off towards the Number 6, I saw him lying there in the grass.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: You have now named three persons. The one you last talked about was shot. What about the two other persons you named? Did you see what kind of -- the effect of the treatment they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, death. That resulted in death. Petko was already dead and Vujcic was dead. As for Gojko Miljanic, he was in a coma. He was unconscious, so we transported him in some kind of a wheelbarrow. It's used in construction work. It's used to transport concrete when you're building things, and we lay him down on a long crate in Number 6 that was used for rifles, to store rifles. He never regained consciousness, and the next afternoon, 24 hours later, he moved about. He uttered some inarticulate sounds and he just died. He stayed with us for 24 hours and he was taken away the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have some more questions about what happened along this wall. You said that different people took turns in beating you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know that, because we were not allowed to turn around. I don't see how just three people could keep doing that for such a long time. I don't know if that was the same group. I managed to see one with the end of my eye. He was a large person, large man, with closely -- with a crew cut. They told me later, those who recognised him, that it was a police officer from the village of Japoluk near Tarcin, ex-police officer. He used to be a police officer in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were you aware of somebody being in command of these people who beat the captured Bradina people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
