utterances.text: I don't know. As for those who arrested us in Bradina, they probably had a commander. As for those in Celebici, whether some of them was a Commander, I don't know. The only thing that I heard a voice admonishing them. It is probably someone in command, that we shouldn't be beaten on the head, because the first group from Bradina had been taken the day before, and they were beaten on the head, on their heads very severely, and when they were transferred to Number 6 the next day, their heads were injured. We were beaten from our necks down to the bottom of our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you said you were taken to building Number 6, Hangar Number 6; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you something about where they were taking you and informing you what was going to happen to you or where you were being kept or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did all of you go to Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: And you named a figure something between 80 and 90. Were there still that amount of people except for the dead, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of all of those, Petko remained there because he was dead. Miroslav Vujcic was also dead and we carried Gojko with us into Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were there any other people in Number 6 when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were the first ones.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: In front of you you have -- if you stand up, you can see a model of the camp, if you will have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to give Mr Gligorevic something to point with, and I will ask him if he can tell us something about where he was placed: my first question is: do you recognise this as a model of the camp in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you point to the wall where you were lined up after your arrival at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were approximately -- this is the wall where it happened, (indicating) this wall here, and then after that we were taken here between the command building and number 22, and we went to Number 6 by this route, and since I entered inside with the first group, I was placed here by this wall, somewhere around the middle of that wall.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down again. Now, your Honours, I would like to introduce a sketch to show that to the witness and I will have that marked for identification. I have copies for the court and for the defence: if authenticated, I plan to tender this as evidence. Mr Gligorevic, do you recognise this sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you make it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: When did you make it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made it at the investigator to whom I gave a statement last year.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: At the time when you were interrogated by a representative from this Tribunal. Thank you. Will you now on this sketch identify -- you can start by identifying the door through which you entered these premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you want me to show?

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: The ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, of course. So if you can diminish it a bit so we can see the whole sketch maybe. A bit more. A bit more. There we are. If you can make it a little higher. There we are. Thank you. Can you start with pointing at the door through which you entered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you then put?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was here at the top, on the opposite end, here, right here near the middle of the shorter wall.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Where there is a cross on the sketch, that's your place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you stay at this place all the time you spent in Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while I was in Celebici that is where I was sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: For how long time was that? When did you leave Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Celebici on 4th October 1992 and then I was transferred to Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So in principle you spent the time from 27th May 1992 to the beginning of October 1992 in this very place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go and sit in any other place in this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were you allowed out every now and then by need of nature or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes, during the first ten days or so, from time to time, but let me tell you right now there was not a great need for that. I don't know what happened, whether it was because of a mental shock or inadequate food. There was virtually no food at all. Many people did not feel the need to defaecate. I, for instance, only went out to defaecate after 13 days, and I was among the first to do so. There were people who did not have a bowel movement for 40 days. I can't understand how a man can bear that, but that was what happened. Some people had a bowel movement after as many as 40 days.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: But when you were allowed out, say, after 13 days, as you say, were you -- did they take you out in groups or one by one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: They took you out in groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: One by one. After you have been outside did somebody follow you out and follow you back?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to the leading form of the questions that he is asking, both of the questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am trying to have the witness tell us what happened, when he has just testified that he stayed in this place, and I will see what exceptions there was from this perpetual staying there. That is all my goal with this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can improve on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will do that. When you were allowed to go out, did someone accompany you back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not an escort, because the guard was nearby. Just behind the hangar on a hill they dug out a septic tank and there were two planks thrown over it and that's where we defecated. As for the urination, we did that into a ditch, a concrete ditch behind the hangar next to a road, and there was water inside that ditch. That was at the beginning. Then later on, when Mr Delic became the Commander, he forbade that and then we were allowed to go out twice a day in his presence, in the morning when he came and then in the evening. As for what it looked like, let me give you an idea. He would say -- he would determine a group of 30-40 people, and they had to line up, and then they had to run out of the hangar, stand next to the ditch and those who were able to urinate, they did that, because it was a very short time, and the next order was: turn around and go back. One was not allowed to linger. My problem was that I was always at the end of this line and I was always the last to go out and I didn't have enough time to do that, but maybe it was also some kind of a psychological block, because I was always expecting this order: "Turn around"; and I found it very hard to do that. So we ran back and then the other group would follow us, and the same procedure was followed at night. In the meantime, whose who felt the need to relieve themselves, if the guard was one of the good ones, and if the Commander was not there in the camp, then they would allow people to go out during the day. If not, then they wouldn't be allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were you ordered to return to the same spot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the same spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are talking about the general conditions in the camp, you may go on and tell us something about the food, water supply and other conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The food was very bad. We would get a piece of bread and at the beginning there was some vegetables too. At first we left -- we went out and there was a crate right next to the door, a rifle crate, and there was an army can of some sort; I don't know what it's called. There were five spoons, and so we would go out in groups of five, and the amount of this too was we could eat about one, two or three spoonfuls and then we would go back and another group would come out. Later on we ate inside. In the time when we were eating outside many people were beaten, so some people did not dare to go out at all. It was very strictly prohibited to take more than what was the ration, and then later on this was also -- we did not receive that. We only received thin slices of bread, 14-16 slices per loaf. Then approximately in mid-July, I think, even the bread grew scarce, and then at one time we did not receive any food for three days. People turned into skeletons. You could hardly recognise them. Many could not even stand up. They had to lean against something, and if they stood up, they would fall down. Then after that we began receiving some more food again. I don't know what the reason was for that, and another problem was water supply.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can imagine this was a hangar made of tin. The roof and the walls were made of tin. There was just a small door and in July and August, you can feel the influence of the Mediterranean climate. It's very hot. It was especially hard for us, for our group. We were placed on the opposite side of the door and the heat was very intense. There was not enough water, although there was water flowing outside without any control.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher to lower the ELMO; I cannot see the witness from the point where I stand. This document, now having been authenticated, I ask permission to tender it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The document is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. On the sketch we could see that there were lots of small dots, being, I suppose, people sitting there. Could you estimate -- you have told us already that there were something like 80 persons brought there in the first place. How many were you at the most in this hangar during your stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, approximately when those from Number 9 were brought in, they had been brought in the day before, and when some other people from the village of Brdjani were brought in for a time, there were about 240 people inside that hangar. These people sat around next to the walls and there were two rows down the middle. These people, for the entire time, when they stayed there they couldn't lean against anything.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. I will now turn your mind to incidents, if any, that took place. Was there some kind of mistreatment of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you please tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many instances of abuse. At the very beginning, I think it was the second or third evening, a group came in. They were looking for people from Sarajevo. A cousin of mine stood up, Stravko Gligorevic -- he really did live in Sarajevo -- and a man by the name of Milosz, who lived in Sekilovic Kolonija in Sarajevo, but he was originally from Bradina. So they answered, and one of them approached this Milosz and said: "Well, we are neighbours. I am also from Sekilovic Kolonija." He wanted to shake hands with Milosz and then he started beating him. He threw him down on to the concrete floor and beat him mercilessly. Another one beat Stravko in the meantime. They picked them up and took them away. We learned later -- I don't know if it is true or not -- that Milosz was killed on Igman and Stravko reached a prison in Strasniza, where he was killed later. For the first ten days there were no mass beatings. That was the period when they were questioning us, some kinds of judges were questioning, and we were giving statements.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can we stay with that for just a moment and you tell the court about this interrogation you were submitted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was like this. I went to see a man in uniform. I did not know him. I do not know if he was a judge. I do not think so. It was done behind the building opposite the building number 22, that was the command building. We squatted down and I had to confirm whatever he put to me. I had to admit that I had a rifle, although I did not have a rifle. I came from Hadzici and I did not have any kind of weapon. I had to also admit that I fired shots, although I didn't. I had to sign in Cyrillic alphabet to make it more credible, although I wanted to sign my name in the Roman alphabet, because you couldn't even -- you couldn't use Cyrillic alphabet at all down there. They simply said whoever was up there had to have a weapon and you had to either sign or to be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: And you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had to.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Was this just a brief interrogation, or did it last for some time? Did they go into details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no details. No details were mentioned. Well, as I already told you, we did that squatting down on the pavement behind that building. It was a confession made under duress that I had a weapon, that I discharged the weapon. Where I was, where I came from. This is just what I was telling you about, that I lived in Hadzici and I went to Bradina, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Was this the only type of interrogation you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, that was the only one. I was not interrogated again.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did they tell you why you were arrested, or did they charge you with any crime at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nobody gave us any explanation, and we were not allowed -- we did not dare to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go back to the incidents that took place during your stay in the Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when those -- let's call them judges but they were not real investigative judges -- when they completed their task, then the prisoners started to suffer. First, they were taken out at night and beaten. This was really horrible. When the night fell, since the door, the entrance door, did not have a lock, we used a wooden plank to prop it up, and then they would put a heavy rifle crate against it, and then when it became really dark, when you heard that plank hit the asphalt, when they started dragging it, dragging the crate along the asphalt, then you knew what would happen. The door would open and they would start calling people out and taking them out. Many people were taken out. They walked in. Then they would put them somewhere, and then the next morning we would sprinkle water over them and if somebody had some salt, they would also apply that to the bruises. So it was really horrible. Every night was a horror. One morning -- I don't know the exact date -- I think it was in mid-June -- they took out Milorad Kuljanin. He was a young man from Bradina. They took him behind the hangar and beat him and then we heard a shot -- two shots I think it was, and they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you say "they took him out", did you ever see somebody special taking anybody out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not see anyone, because I was up there on the opposite end of the hangar, and at that time the first group, that was my group, we were going out for urination in the morning, but some of the group were already out there and one of them who saw that was Zjelko Cecez, and he was killed that same evening.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you see that killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was inside. I was sitting at my place.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: You said that at night it was usual that somebody was called out and guards came to take somebody. Can you estimate how many times that happened, that prisoners were taken out at night? Any way of estimating how many times this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it happened many times, virtually every evening. I remember very clearly the night when they were taking people out there was a thunderstorm, a really bad thunderstorm, and that night nobody was taken out. The door was not opened, and we were very happy about that, and that was because of the thunderstorm; nobody could be taken out because of that. It lasted until, with some brief interruptions, until the arrival of the Red Cross, and during that period, in addition to the two people I mentioned, Milorad Kuljanin and Zjelko Cecez, Simo Jovanovic was also killed, and so was Scepo Gotovac, Nedjo Magazin and Bosko Samoukovic, and Zjelko Klimenta, I think, nicknamed Keljo.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: You have now named some of the people who were killed. Did you yourself witness some of these killings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally saw -- well, in fact, 240 people at least saw that. That was the killing of Bosko Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you tell us about what you and the others saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened in this way. The guard in our prison -- I think his name is Esad and last name Landzo, nicknamed Zenga, he would enter virtually every day when his shift was on. It was from noon on. He entered the hangar and then he would pick out somebody, and he would beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would beat them inside the hangar or outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning at night when they were taking people out at night, in which he took part, he would not come into the hangar, because we were a lot in there. There was no light in there, so maybe he did not dare. Later the beating started in day-time, and people were taken out and people were tortured. They were burnt. Their ears were pierced. People were forced to eat grass, and there were false executions. But all these other things he did inside. People in camouflage uniform came. They introduced themselves as having come from Mostar. Whenever somebody would come from outside, we would have to get up and stand very still, ready, and look down then, awaiting who they were going to beat, who knows for what reason. One of them said his speciality was that the prisoner would lie down and do push-ups, and whenever he would raise himself, he would kick him. After he left, the same practice was used by the same guard, Zenga, and that became his speciality. The other speciality was the plank that I said was used to close the door. I don't know how. It was about 1.2 metres, about 5 cms thick, 10 cms wide, which he would turn so that the narrower side would be down, and the prisoner would have to come to where we were taking food, and he would have to stand there, and he would beat him in the rib cage area.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: You say "he" would beat him. Who was "he" in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking about this guard Zenga, Esad Landzo. Bosko was taken out the same way. He put his hands behind his -- on his neck behind. He beat him a number of times. He was moaning and then finally he fell down and started to mumble, gurgle, and then he was taken out so that he could come to a little bit. However, he continued to gurgle. Then they took him to this Number 22 and shortly thereafter he died.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Who was that person you now talked about? Did you give a name to him? I did not get it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour that is asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I did not get it, so for my information I would like to hear it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What was the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Bosko was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It has come on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. You have now told the court about the different kinds of methods used to mistreat detainees. Was this an exhaustive account of the methods used to mistreat them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. One of the specialities of this guard Zenga was to burn people. For instance, to Dusko Bendjo, and I saw this with my own eyes, that is Zenga, at that time he always had a little bottle filled with gasoline. Then he would -- he poured -- from the knee down to the ankles he poured this gasoline and set it on fire and did not allow him to put it out, so later terrible wounds developed and we all thought that he would lose both of his legs. I think he still must have bad scars from it. He also burnt -- that was the next thing. Sometimes he would burn paper. Then he would heat a knife on it and then he forces the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. Did this person say he saw this second occurrence that he is talking about, personally viewed it, or is he speaking from something that he has heard from somebody else? This next incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why do you not allow them to interpret what he is saying? Let us hear him before you object.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would just like to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him make his statement. Then if you object, we will hear your objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then it is too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How do you object when you do not even hear what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It all happened inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please state what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please go on and tell us: what you now have accounted for, did that take place in the hangar or outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Dusko Bendjo, that was in the hangar and we all watched it. Some others, like Nedjelko Draganic and Spasoje Miljanic, to them it was happening outside. Later on we all saw big wounds and blisters on hands. I personally saw when to Mirko Djordjic, who was about two, three places away from me in the same row, when he burst his ear with a pincer. He couldn't hear. He often beat him and he didn't bother to take them out to the door but he would just beat them right there. He would say: "Come and do push-ups." Then he started kicking him. To Momir Kuljanin he was burning palms. He had big blisters on his palms for days.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you ever witness any sexual assaults to people? If you saw this, please do not use any names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That too happened. Some time in mid-July they brought in two young men, whom I knew very well, because I was their teacher in Bradina. They were two brothers. They were singled out by Zenga for torture. He beat them and then they had to slap each other's face, for instance, and if the slaps were not strong enough, then he would show them how it's really done. One day they had to suck each other's penis.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Again who is "he" in this account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the guard Esad Landzo, Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did this take place just once or did it happen more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The beatings were very frequent, and the things I am saying about, that sexual abuse, that was once, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you some questions about how this camp was run. Have you any idea who was the Commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as we knew, and in the beginning we didn't know, I know that Hazim Delic was there every day. I assume, and later we heard from the guards as well, that he was the Deputy Commander of the camp. Who the Commander was, at first I really don't know. I later heard that it was Mr Pavo Mucic. However, he really would come very seldom to Number 6, and I did not know him from before. I assume that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you see any of these now named persons exercising command in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Delic, because we all had to obey him, because all the guards had to obey him, and they were even afraid of him. I don't know about Pavo Mucic. I cannot recall when I saw him for the first time. I cannot remember exactly, but I think it was somewhere late June or early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can interrupt please for a moment? I can see that the transcription is not recording accurately the translation that was given. It says "I cannot remember whether I saw him for the first time." The answer given was: "I cannot remember when I saw him for the first time." I am anxious to make that clear. That is not a correct transcription.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What he said in the transcript is: "I can't remember exactly but I saw him late in June and July." That has come in the record. That has come in the record. That is a fair translation of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am anxious about the earlier use of the word "whether" in the transcript. That is not what was translated. It was "when" was the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is "whether I saw him for the first time".

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is what I heard being said over the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am grateful to my learned friend Mr Ostberg for saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That leads me to the question: did you see him many times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Repeat the question and let him say what he wanted to say. Repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then I repeat my question this way: did you see Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him, but I cannot determine the exact time. I think it was somewhere at the end of June or early July, when the first groups were being transferred to Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you then continuously see him? I mean, to what extent did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to Number 6 rather infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Rather infrequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, relatively seldom, but he was in charge of the camp, the Camp Commander. You could infer that from the guards who referred to him when he would arrive on a motorcycle, and he arrived on motorcycles: "Here comes the Commander", and everybody had to be in their places. Even if there was beating going on, that would stop, and the prisoner would be put back into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us about if and in what way you saw Mr Delic exercising his command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was obvious. There was no question there. I would say all guards -- as I said, all guards were afraid. When he was there, they all had to be in their places and in front of him. We had to get up when he would enter the hangar. We had to stand at attention and look down before us. We couldn't look straight, and from all that we inferred that he had a certain function and then later we heard that he was a Deputy Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. Did he use to come to Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He would come very often.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you tell us about some -- were there some obvious reasons for his visits to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably to control his guards, to control us, and to abuse us. Delic was one of those who also took a lot of people out and beat them also inside the hangar itself too. Sometimes he beat everybody one by one. Sometimes he would skip someone. Sometimes he had his own, as we called it, patients, and he beat them only, like Dusko Bendjo, Vukasin Mrkajic. Most often those were the blows: "Turn around, put your hands on your neck", and then he would hit them a few times, or even, because this Mrkajic was in the middle row, he didn't have to get up. He would just sit and he would hit him. It came to the point where Mrkajic's ribs were fractured and blue, and when Delic would come in, he would start begging: "Please don't, Mr Commander."

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you specify how he hit them? With hands or with some instrument or in what way this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most often he would kick them and when there were mass beatings, most often he used whatever he had, either a broomstick or a shovel, which would be somewhere around, something that was at hand. Sometimes he would have two -- sometimes he would break two handles against the bodies of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just a moment, your Honour. I am just checking my papers. I will ask again about Delic. You named he used swords and you mentioned also -- I have to check -- can you remember other instruments he used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I mentioned is what he used most frequently. For a while, it is interesting, and that was only for one prisoner, he used a gadget which produced electric shocks. That was used on Davor Kuljanin. He used that rarely on anybody else. What we remembered in particular was that famous baseball bat, which he carried around a long time, and when he showed up in the hangar with it, it was then known that somebody was going to get beaten with it.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you described this, have you any possibility to remember in which time-frame it took place? Was this some special time during your stay in Celebici? If you can try to name a month or length of time from this treatment from Delic, so we know how to place it in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was during the summer, I think in July and in August, when he carried that out. I don't know exactly when it was when he brought it in the first time, but it was present for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: A long time is a very general description. Could you tell us: are we talking weeks, a month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About a month and a half maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: You told us a lot of mistreatment committed by Zenga, Esad Landzo. Can you also put that in a time period of some kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these crimes, the killings, happened between mid-June until early August. In the second half of July I believe Milorad Kuljanin and Zjelko Cecez and Scepo Gotovac were killed, as well as Simo Jovanovic and Nedjo Milosevic, and I think somewhere towards the end in the second half of July there was also the killing of Bosko Samoukovic, and around that time, right after that is correct, I think it was just after that, Zjelko Klimenta was killed. That's about the time period. I forgot to mention a strange death. That was Cedo Avramovic, who was with us several nights only. He was arrested somewhere in Konjic and brought there. We did not hear anybody coming in and leaving. It was totally dark and everybody was asleep. I heard some rumble and something like a running between the rows, and then I heard some dangling, something like as if there was a wire, as if a wire was rubbed against some metal object, and then there was a blunt blow, and then everything was quiet, and in the morning when it grew light between the rows Cedo's clothes were folded. It was very neat, as if it was going to be put in a suitcase, and several metres away from me he was there lying dead, stripped to the waist. What happened we never knew. We speculated that he just went insane and that's what happened, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: So there was no-one in the Hangar Number 6 to kill him or to reach this effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We really literally didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: You mentioned initially that you stayed in this camp until 4th October 1992. Can you tell us what -- the circumstances around your leaving the premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Occasionally groups of 20 or 30 people would be transferred to the Musala prison in Konjic. Usually the Commander would come, the camp Commander, Mr Pavo Mucic, and the Deputy, Mr Delic, and then we all had to stand at attention and they determined who they were going to transfer to that camp in Musala. My turn came. I was selected and on 4th October we were transferred to Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: How long did you stay there then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed until 6th October 1994, so I don't know what period it is. About two years. Otherwise I was there two years, four months and nine days in total.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. I am ready to conclude my -- have I missed some? Maybe. Mr Gligorevic, you have in your account mentioned many names of people being killed, but in some instances you haven't given any direct details of what happened, what you saw yourself or heard yourself. That brings me back to take up some of these names to put some questions to you. I have three persons on this list and I ask your Honours if that maybe could be put on when we continue examining this witness, the time now being 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you had reached the end of your examination-in-chief, but since you are still continuing we will then have to adjourn until Tuesday at 10.00 am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You will have to continue to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, before I give it to the cross-examination. We will still have him nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is as far as we can go today. The witness is still available so when he comes on Tuesday, we will continue with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will now adjourn until Tuesday at 10.00 am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: --ooOoo--

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until Tuesday morning at 10.00 am)
